title: WHAT JUDAS AND GEHAZI HAD IN COMMON
paragraphs: WHAT JUDAS AND GEHAZI HAD IN COMMON
Some betrayals do not begin with hatred.
They begin with small compromises nobody notices.

A hidden desire.
A private justification.
A secret attachment.
Long before Judas kissed Jesus in the garden, something else had already kissed his heart.
Long before Gehazi chased Naaman down the road, something else had already been running through his soul.
One stood near the servant of God.
And the terrifying truth is that neither man collapsed overnight.
The seeds of destruction had been growing quietly for a long time.
That is what makes their stories so dangerous.
Because many Christians think spiritual failure begins when a person commits a public sin.
Public collapse is usually the harvest.
Yet when their lives are placed side by side, the similarities become impossible to ignore.
Not because they committed identical sins.
But because they surrendered to the same master.
The love of what they could gain.
The apostle Paul would later write:
The belief that something God has not given you would satisfy you more than God Himself.
The Hebrew text gives us a glimpse into Gehazi's heart.
In 2 Kings 5, Naaman the Syrian had been healed of leprosy through the power of God.
Overwhelmed with gratitude, Naaman offered gifts to Elisha.
The miracle had been given freely.
God's grace could not be purchased.
And suddenly the servant wanted what the prophet rejected.

"But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, 'My master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not accepting from his hand what he brought. As Yahweh lives, I will run after him and get something from him.'" (2 Kings 5:20)
The Hebrew phrase is deeply revealing.
Gehazi literally chased what God had chosen not to give him.
Many believers are still doing the same thing.
Running after relationships God did not assign.
Running after recognition God did not promise.
Running after wealth God did not provide.
Running after opportunities God never opened.
The tragedy was not merely that Gehazi wanted money.
The tragedy was that he wanted money more than he wanted obedience.
That is always where spiritual disaster begins.
John's Gospel provides one of the most shocking descriptions of his character.
When Mary poured expensive perfume upon Jesus, Judas objected.
But John exposed the real motive.
"He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief..." (John 12:6)
Someone who secretly takes what belongs to another.
The betrayal in Gethsemane did not begin in Gethsemane.
Sin always asks for secrecy before it demands surrender.
That is why both men appeared faithful until the very end.
Gehazi still wore the appearance of a servant.
Judas still wore the appearance of a disciple.
The greatest spiritual threats rarely arrive wearing obvious darkness.
They arrive disguised as acceptable desires.
The desire to finally get what we think we deserve.
Both men reached the moment where hidden sin became visible.
When Elisha confronted Gehazi, the prophet asked:
"Did not my heart go when the man turned from his chariot to meet you?" (2 Kings 5:26)
Likewise, Jesus knew exactly what Judas was becoming.
Years before the betrayal, Jesus said:
"Did I not choose you, the Twelve? And yet one of you is a devil." (John 6:70)
Judas spent years near Jesus while simultaneously drifting away from Him.
Physical proximity does not equal spiritual intimacy.
Someone can attend church every week and still be moving farther from God.
Someone can serve in ministry and still be nurturing secret idols.
Someone can know theology and still be starving spiritually.
Neither truly conquered the idol within.
Both stories stand as warning signs across Scripture.
But perhaps the greatest lesson is not about greed.
Because greed is never ultimately about money.
Greed is worship directed toward something other than God.
Every temptation asks the same question:
That was the question before Gehazi.
That was the question before Judas.
That is the question before us.
The Gospel presents a breathtaking contrast.
Jesus purchased sinners with His blood.
Christ endured the cross for everlasting redemption.
Both men reached for what would eventually perish.
The Savior offered what could never be lost.
This is why repentance matters so urgently.
Not because God delights in exposing sinners.
But because He loves rescuing them.
Maybe that is why these stories linger in the soul.
Most believers can find pieces of Gehazi in themselves.
Many can find pieces of Judas.
Moments when we wanted something more than obedience.
Moments when we chased what God never assigned.
Moments when secret compromise felt harmless.
Moments when our hearts quietly drifted.
But this is where grace enters.
You are still being invited back.
The same Jesus who knew Judas completely still washed his feet.
The same God who exposed sin throughout Scripture still calls sinners to repentance today.
Your honesty may become the encouragement someone else desperately needed to see.
One hidden desire can destroy a life—but one surrendered heart can change eternity.
